_doc: Formulary spider grounding — drug-covers-organism + CSF penetration facts grounded in primary sources with verbatim byte-quotes + independent re-extraction. status grounded = source affirms + re-extraction-stable + entailed; refuted = source contradicts the authored fact; unclear/grounded_unstable = flagged.

records.claim: vancomycin provides reliable antimicrobial coverage of ceftriaxone-nonsusceptible (resistant) Streptococcus pneumoniae (in the context of treating bacterial meningitis / serious infection).

grounded.source_title: Management of Bacterial Meningitis: New Guidelines from the IDSA (AAFP summary of Tunkel et al., IDSA Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis)
grounded.byte_quote: In patients with meningitis caused by penicillin- or cephalosporin-resistant strains it may be used in combination with a third-generation cephalosporin but should not be used alone (A-III).
grounded.note: The fact claims vancomycin provides RELIABLE standalone coverage of ceftriaxone-/cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae in meningitis. The IDSA guideline (summarized by AAFP) explicitly refutes vancomycin monotherapy: for penicillin-/cephalosporin-resistant strains vancomycin "may be used in combination with a third-generation cephalosporin but should not be used alone (A-III)." Vancomycin IS active in vitro against these resistant pneumococci, but it is NOT reliable as sole therapy for CNS infection because of inconsistent CSF penetration — the guideline mandates combination with a third-gen cephalosporin (commonly plus rifampin when dexamethasone is co-administered). So the in vitro coverage claim is partly true, but the clinical claim of "reliable coverage" for serious infection/meningitis is refuted as stated. A grounded version would be: "vancomycin is active against ceftriaxone-resistant S. pneumoniae but must be combined with a third-generation cephalosporin for meningitis."

verification.quote_reextracted: In patients with meningitis caused by penicillin- or cephalosporin-resistant strains it may be used in combination with a third-generation cephalosporin but should not be used alone (A-III).
verification.note: Re-extraction is stable: the identical passage was located on an independent WebFetch of the AAFP/IDSA-guidelines page, including corroborating sentences ("use of vancomycin is not recommended ... non-resistant strains" (E-II); dexamethasone-CSF-vancomycin efficacy concern). However, the source does NOT entail the claim as worded. The claim asserts vancomycin "provides RELIABLE antimicrobial coverage" of ceftriaxone-nonsusceptible S. pneumoniae. The source's actual recommendation is the opposite emphasis: for resistant strains vancomycin "may be used in combination with a third-generation cephalosporin but SHOULD NOT BE USED ALONE (A-III)." A guideline that explicitly forbids monotherapy and mandates combination with a cephalosporin is not asserting that vancomycin is reliable standalone coverage; the dexamethasone-may-inhibit-CSF-vancomycin caveat further signals concern about its reliability in the CNS. So while vancomycin is part of the resistant-strain regimen, the source does not support "reliable coverage" — it supports "use only in combination, never alone." Claim overstates; entailment fails.

records.claim: vancomycin provides reliable antimicrobial coverage of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) (in the context of treating bacterial meningitis / serious infection).

grounded.source_title: Clinical Practice Guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America for the Treatment of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Infections in Adults and Children (Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2011;52(3):e18–e55)
grounded.byte_quote: IV vancomycin for 2 weeks is recommended (B-II).
grounded.note: IDSA MRSA treatment guideline (CID 2011) — Section VI, Meningitis subsection (recommendation 49) — recommends IV vancomycin as therapy for MRSA meningitis. Throughout the guideline vancomycin is the primary recommended agent for serious/CNS MRSA infections (also rated A-II/A-I for bacteremia and endocarditis), confirming vancomycin provides reliable coverage of MRSA in serious infection / meningitis. Supports the FACT.

verification.quote_reextracted: Vancomycin has been the mainstay of parenteral therapy for MRSA infections. ... For CNS/meningitis: "IV vancomycin for 2 weeks is recommended (B-II)."
verification.note: Source is the IDSA 2011 Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of MRSA Infections (Liu et al., CID 52:3, e18). Independent re-extraction (direct WebFetch + corroborating WebSearch) reproduces the prior finding. The document explicitly frames vancomycin as the standard/mainstay anti-MRSA agent ("Vancomycin has been the mainstay of parenteral therapy for MRSA infections") and, in the CNS-infection section, recommends "IV vancomycin for 2 weeks is recommended (B-II)" for MRSA meningitis, plus high-dose serious-infection dosing (15-20 mg/kg q8-12h). The entire document is, by title, about treating MRSA, so the subject (vancomycin) covering the object (MRSA) in the meningitis/serious-infection context is directly entailed, not inferred. One honest caveat the source itself raises (does not negate the claim): it advises considering an alternative agent if vancomycin MIC is >=1-2 ug/mL, i.e. coverage is "reliable" as first-line but susceptibility-dependent. The prior quote is accurate and on-point. re_extraction_stable=true, entails=true.

records.claim: vancomycin achieves therapeutic concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (adequate CNS/CSF penetration to treat meningitis).

grounded.source_title: VANCOMYCIN HYDROCHLORIDE FOR INJECTION, USP — FDA Label (Clinical Pharmacology), DailyMed
grounded.byte_quote: Vancomycin does not readily diffuse across normal meninges into the spinal fluid; but, when the meninges are inflamed, penetration into the spinal fluid occurs.
grounded.note: FDA label (authoritative primary source) confirms vancomycin penetration into spinal fluid occurs WHEN meninges are inflamed — i.e., in meningitis — but does NOT readily diffuse across normal meninges. This is equivocal relative to the fact's claim of "therapeutic/adequate" CSF concentrations: the label affirms that penetration occurs in the inflamed (meningitis) state that the fact concerns, but stops short of asserting therapeutic adequacy. Corroborating primary literature (IDSA 2017 healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis guideline, PMC5848239; systematic reviews PubMed 28528396) characterizes IV vancomycin CSF penetration as limited (~1% uninflamed, ~5% inflamed; CSF:serum ratio ~18-48%) and recommends therapeutic drug monitoring and intraventricular dosing for difficult cases — so "adequate therapeutic CNS penetration" as a flat claim is not cleanly grounded. Verdict 'unclear': the affirming span is real and source-grounded for the inflamed-meninges condition, but the strength implied by the fact (reliably therapeutic) is not supported. supports=true reflects that the cited span affirms penetration in the meningitis scenario.

verification.quote_reextracted: Vancomycin does not readily diffuse across normal meninges into the spinal fluid; but, when the meninges are inflamed, penetration into the spinal fluid occurs.
verification.note: Independent WebFetch of the DailyMed label returned the identical passage in the CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY section — re-extraction is stable. However, the source does NOT entail the claim as stated. The claim asserts vancomycin "achieves therapeutic concentrations" / "adequate CNS/CSF penetration to treat meningitis." The label only states qualitatively that (a) vancomycin does NOT readily diffuse across NORMAL meninges, and (b) when meninges are INFLAMED, "penetration into the spinal fluid occurs." "Penetration occurs" is a qualitative statement and does not establish that concentrations are THERAPEUTIC or ADEQUATE to treat meningitis, and the unconditional claim ignores the normal-meninges caveat (penetration is poor absent inflammation). The source is at best partial/conditional support, not entailment of the adequacy claim.

grounded.byte_quote: Empirical therapy for suspected meningococcal disease should include an extended-spectrum cephalosporin, such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone.
grounded.note: CDC clinical guidance for meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) recommends ceftriaxone as both empirical and definitive therapy. grounded.source_title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis (IDSA; Tunkel et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases 2004)
grounded.byte_quote: In patients with H. influenzae type b meningitis, the emergence of β-lactamase—producing strains and resistance to chloramphenicol has made these agents the drugs of choice for empirical therapy for H. influenzae meningitis, pending results of in vitro susceptibility testing.
grounded.note: "These agents" refers to third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone), which the IDSA bacterial meningitis guideline names as the drugs of choice for empirical therapy of H. influenzae meningitis. The IDSA pathogen-specific recommendations also list ceftriaxone (a 3rd-gen cephalosporin) as standard therapy for H. influenzae type b. This directly affirms that ceftriaxone provides reliable coverage of H. influenzae in serious infection/meningitis. Source = IDSA primary guideline.

verification.quote_reextracted: In patients with H. influenzae type b meningitis, the emergence of β-lactamase-producing strains and resistance to chloramphenicol has made these agents the drugs of choice for empirical therapy for H. influenzae meningitis, pending results of in vitro susceptibility testing.
verification.note: Independent re-fetch of the OUP CID article (IDSA Practical Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis, Tunkel et al. 2004) reproduces the prior quote verbatim. The antecedent "these agents" = the third-generation cephalosporins, established by the immediately preceding sentence: "The treatment of bacterial meningitis has been revolutionized by the availability of the third-generation cephalosporins." Ceftriaxone is one of the two third-gen cephalosporins named (alongside cefotaxime) and they are used interchangeably in the empirical-therapy recommendations (e.g., "vancomycin combined with either cefotaxime or ceftriaxone"). The source therefore declares ceftriaxone (as a third-gen cephalosporin) a drug of choice for H. influenzae meningitis, including against β-lactamase-producing strains — which entails reliable antimicrobial coverage of H. influenzae in the meningitis/serious-infection context. One caveat: the source attributes the "drugs of choice" status to the third-gen cephalosporin class generically rather than singling out ceftriaxone by name in this specific sentence, but ceftriaxone's membership in that class and its explicit listing as an empirical option make the entailment hold.

grounded.source_title: Penicillin-Susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae Meningitis in Adults: Does the Ceftriaxone Dosing Matter? (PMC10215215)
grounded.byte_quote: After S. pneumoniae is isolated and the penicillin susceptibility of the causative strain is confirmed, antibiotic treatment should be streamlined to either penicillin or ceftriaxone (or ampicillin, amoxicillin, or cefotaxime).
grounded.note: Primary source: peer-reviewed PMC clinical article on penicillin-susceptible S. pneumoniae meningitis in adults. It affirms ceftriaxone as a recommended directed/streamlined therapy once penicillin susceptibility is confirmed, and separately reports "All isolates were susceptible to ceftriaxone," confirming reliable in-vitro coverage. This grounds the FACT that ceftriaxone provides reliable coverage of penicillin-susceptible S. pneumoniae in the meningitis/serious-infection context. (IDSA 2004 guidelines corroborate third-gen cephalosporins for pneumococcal meningitis; this source is the most directly on-point for the penicillin-susceptible subgroup.)

verification.quote_reextracted: After S. pneumoniae is isolated and the penicillin susceptibility of the causative strain is confirmed, antibiotic treatment should be streamlined to either penicillin or ceftriaxone (or ampicillin, amoxicillin, or cefotaxime).

records.claim: ampicillin provides reliable antimicrobial coverage of Escherichia coli (in the context of treating bacterial meningitis / serious infection).

grounded.source_title: Trends in Antibiotic Resistance of Escherichia coli Strains Isolated from Clinical Samples (2019–2023): A Hospital-Based Retrospective Analysis (PMC12472492)
grounded.byte_quote: In 2020, ampicillin resistance among E. coli isolates rose to over 55%, confirming the persistent inefficacy of this agent.
grounded.note: The FACT claims ampicillin provides RELIABLE coverage of E. coli. A PMC peer-reviewed retrospective surveillance study refutes this: ampicillin resistance among E. coli isolates exceeded 55% in 2020 and remained the highest of all tested agents across 2019–2023 (>48% every year), with the authors stating the data confirm "the persistent inefficacy of this agent" and that ampicillin "should be avoided for empirical treatment." Corroborated by IDSA bacterial-meningitis guidance, where empiric gram-negative (including E. coli) coverage is provided by third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone), NOT ampicillin — ampicillin is added only for Listeria monocytogenes coverage. Note: a minority of E. coli isolates remain ampicillin-susceptible, but the agent does not provide RELIABLE empiric coverage, so the fact as stated is refuted.

verification.quote_reextracted: In 2020, ampicillin resistance among E. coli isolates rose to over 55%, confirming the persistent inefficacy of this agent.
verification.note: Independent re-fetch of PMC12472492 reproduces the prior quote verbatim (re-extraction stable). The source CONTRADICTS the claim: it reports ampicillin resistance among E. coli exceeding 48% in every year 2019-2023 (>55% in 2020), describing ampicillin as having "limited therapeutic value" / "persistent inefficacy" and recommending it "should be avoided for empirical treatment." Therefore the source's words do NOT entail that ampicillin provides reliable coverage of E. coli — they entail the opposite, so entails=false. Caveat: the article's clinical context is uncomplicated UTIs in a Romanian hospital, not bacterial meningitis as framed in the FACT; the surveillance data is a microbiological resistance fact that bears on the claim but is not meningitis-specific.

grounded.source_title: Tunkel AR, et al. Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis. Clinical Infectious Diseases (IDSA), 2004;39(9):1267-1284
grounded.byte_quote: A fourth-generation cephalosporin, cefepime, has been shown to be safe and therapeutically equivalent to cefotaxime in the treatment of bacterial meningitis in infants and children.
grounded.note: PRIMARY SOURCE: IDSA 2004 bacterial-meningitis guideline (Tunkel et al., CID). The verbatim quoted sentence (read from the full text) establishes cefepime as a fourth-generation cephalosporin therapeutically EQUIVALENT to cefotaxime for bacterial meningitis. Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone are the gold-standard agents for N. meningitidis, and IDSA Table 5 lists cefepime among acceptable alternative agents for meningococcal meningitis (the table itself is rendered as an image and could not be transcribed verbatim via fetch). CORROBORATION: a PMC meningococcal-meningitis review (PMC4922928) and the IDSA healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis guideline both treat cefepime as an extended-spectrum beta-lactam appropriate in CNS infection. CAVEAT / partial counter-signal: the FDA Maxipime (cefepime) package insert, 2012 revision (accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2012/050679s036lbl.pdf), does NOT list Neisseria meningitidis in either its clinically-validated or in-vitro-only spectrum lists, and UK/NICE meningococcal evidence reviews (NBK604080/NBK604081) and a Canadian PMC review do not name cefepime among meningococcal options (they emphasize penicillin G, cefotaxime/ceftriaxone, meropenem, chloramphenicol). This is an omission, not a stated lack of activity. Net: cefepime reliably covers N. meningitidis pharmacologically and is an IDSA-sanctioned alternative, so the FACT is GROUNDED, though it is a second-line/alternative rather than first-line meningococcal agent.

verification.quote_reextracted: A fourth-generation cephalosporin, cefepime, has been shown to be safe and therapeutically equivalent to cefotaxime in the treatment of bacterial meningitis in infants and children.
verification.note: Re-extraction stable: the prior quote appears verbatim in the article's "Cephalosporins" section. However, the source does NOT strictly entail the specific claim about N. meningitidis coverage. The quote only asserts general therapeutic equivalence to cefotaxime for bacterial meningitis in infants/children; it never names Neisseria meningitidis in connection with cefepime. The only organisms the passage explicitly attributes to cefepime are Enterobacter species and Pseudomonas aeruginosa ("greater in vitro activity than the third-generation cephalosporins against Enterobacter species and Pseudomonas aeruginosa"). The article's pathogen-specific recommendations for N. meningitidis list third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone), not cefepime. Coverage of N. meningitidis by cefepime is a plausible clinical inference (equivalence-to-cefotaxime + fourth-gen spectrum), but it is an inference the reader must supply, not something the quoted source words state. Marking entails=false because the entailment requires external pharmacologic knowledge, not the source's words alone.

grounded.source_title: Aztreonam for Injection, USP — FDA Prescribing Information (Pfizer label)
grounded.byte_quote: For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a single 2 g intravenous dose produces serum levels that exceed the MIC90 for approximately 4 to 6 hours.
grounded.note: FDA prescribing information (Pfizer Aztreonam for Injection, USP) confirms aztreonam covers Pseudomonas aeruginosa: it lists P. aeruginosa among susceptible Gram-negative aerobes and as an indicated pathogen across UTI, lower respiratory, septicemia, skin/skin-structure, and intra-abdominal infections; the cited pharmacokinetic line shows serum levels exceeding the P. aeruginosa MIC90. Caveat not contradicting the fact: aztreonam is a monobactam with reliable Gram-negative aerobic (incl. P. aeruginosa) activity but NO Gram-positive or anaerobic coverage — relevant for empiric meningitis where it would be combined, and resistance/MIC variability exists clinically.

verification.quote_reextracted: Aztreonam has been shown to be active against most strains of the following microorganisms...Pseudomonas aeruginosa. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a single 2 g intravenous dose produces serum levels that exceed the MIC90 for approximately 4 to 6 hours.
verification.note: Independent WebFetch of the Pfizer/Hospira Aztreonam for Injection USP label reproduces the prior quote verbatim and finds stronger corroboration: P. aeruginosa is explicitly listed among organisms aztreonam is "active against most strains of," and the drug is indicated for P. aeruginosa infections (lower respiratory tract, septicemia, etc.), with "2 g every six or eight hours recommended... because of the serious nature of infections due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa." The core claim (aztreonam covers P. aeruginosa) is clearly entailed. Caveat on the parenthetical meningitis framing: this label does NOT list meningitis/CNS as an indication and reports only limited CSF penetration (3 mcg/mL with inflamed meninges, Table 1), so the source does not support reliable CNS/meningitis coverage specifically — but the FACT's antimicrobial-coverage assertion itself is entailed.

records.claim: aztreonam achieves therapeutic concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (adequate CNS/CSF penetration to treat meningitis).

grounded.source_title: Penetration of aztreonam into cerebrospinal fluid of patients with and without inflamed meninges (Antimicrob Agents Chemother)
grounded.byte_quote: Aztreonam concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid in the presence of normal and inflamed meninges exceeded the inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations for most gram-negative bacteria.
grounded.note: Primary clinical PK source (Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy). In 34 patients given a single 2 g IV dose, CSF aztreonam exceeded inhibitory/bactericidal concentrations for most gram-negative bacteria; levels were 4x higher with inflamed meninges, and authors concluded a 2 g IV q6h regimen is appropriate for clinical trials of gram-negative bacillary meningitis. Corroborated by PMID 4040132 (J Antimicrob Chemother), which states CSF penetration with meningeal inflammation "appears adequate to warrant" therapeutic trials. Caveat: efficacy is gram-negative-specific (aztreonam has no gram-positive coverage), and viral-meningitis CSF levels were notably lower.

verification.quote_reextracted: Aztreonam concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid in the presence of normal and inflamed meninges exceeded the inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations for most gram-negative bacteria.
verification.note: Independent WebFetch of PMID 6542765 reproduces the prior quote verbatim. Article title: "Penetration of aztreonam into cerebrospinal fluid of patients with and without inflamed meninges." Multiple corroborating sentences support entailment: aztreonam was detected in CSF 1h post-infusion; CSF levels were 4x higher with inflamed meninges; concentrations exceeded MIC/MBC for most gram-negative bacteria in both normal AND inflamed meninges; authors recommend a 2-g IV q6h regimen for clinical trials treating gram-negative bacillary meningitis. Caveat (does not break entailment but worth noting for precision): the therapeutic adequacy is specifically for gram-negative organisms — aztreonam is a monobactam with no gram-positive coverage, so the claim's general "treat meningitis" should be read as gram-negative meningitis. The source clearly entails adequate CSF/CNS penetration to treat susceptible (gram-negative) meningitis.

records.claim: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole provides reliable antimicrobial coverage of Listeria monocytogenes (in the context of treating bacterial meningitis / serious infection).

grounded.source_title: Listeria Monocytogenes — Johns Hopkins ABX Guide
grounded.byte_quote: TMP/SMX is the preferred drug in patients who cannot take ampicillin. This combination has good in vitro activity and is bactericidal vs. Listeria.
grounded.note: The Johns Hopkins ABX Guide (Listeria Monocytogenes monograph) affirms that TMP-SMX has good in vitro activity and is bactericidal against Listeria, and is the preferred agent in patients who cannot take ampicillin; it lists TMP/SMX 3-5 mg/kg (trimethoprim) q6h IV x >=3 wks as an alternative meningitis regimen. This is consistent with IDSA bacterial-meningitis guidance, which lists TMP-SMX as the alternative to penicillin G/ampicillin for L. monocytogenes (notably for beta-lactam-allergic patients). Corroborating real-world use: the PMC nationwide Listeria-meningitis cohort (PMC10050789) reports cotrimoxazole was used to treat patients with amoxicillin allergy. Caveat: TMP-SMX is an ALTERNATIVE, not first-line; ampicillin/penicillin G (+/- gentamicin) remains preferred.

verification.quote_reextracted: TMP/SMX is the preferred drug in patients who cannot take ampicillin. This combination has good in vitro activity and is bactericidal vs. Listeria.
verification.note: Independent WebFetch of the Johns Hopkins ABX Guide Listeria page reproduces the prior quote verbatim. Source additionally lists TMP/SMX as an alternative meningitis regimen ("TMP/SMX 3-5mg/kg (trimethoprim) q6h IV x >=3wks") and notes it is bactericidal whereas ampicillin is "allegedly bacteriostatic," and that cephalosporins/vancomycin lack Listeria activity while TMP/SMX retains it. The source's words (good in vitro activity, bactericidal vs. Listeria, preferred drug when ampicillin cannot be used, explicit meningitis dosing) entail that TMP-SMX provides reliable antimicrobial coverage of L. monocytogenes in serious infection/meningitis. Finding is stable on independent read; entailment holds.

records.claim: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieves therapeutic concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (adequate CNS/CSF penetration to treat meningitis).

grounded.source_title: The Blood–Brain Barrier and Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Optimization of Antibiotics for the Treatment of Central Nervous System Infections in Adults (PMC9774927)
grounded.byte_quote: At doses of 20 mg/kg/day (based on TMP component) divided every 6–12 h, TMP-SMX is an agent qualified for use for CNS infections caused by susceptible bacterial pathogens.
grounded.note: Peer-reviewed PMC pharmacokinetic review (Antibiotics, 2022). TMP-SMX CSF penetration measured at 18% (TMP) and 12% (SMX) of serum; CSF concentrations of TMP 0.5-3.2 mg/L and SMX 5-40 mg/L at 20 mg/kg/day exceed MIC for susceptible pathogens. The review explicitly states TMP-SMX is "qualified for use for CNS infections" including Listeria monocytogenes meningitis and resistant gram-negative meningitis. Affirms adequate CNS/CSF penetration to treat meningitis caused by susceptible organisms.

verification.quote_reextracted: At doses of 20 mg/kg/day (based on TMP component) divided every 6–12 h, TMP-SMX is an agent qualified for use for CNS infections caused by susceptible bacterial pathogens.
verification.note: Independent WebFetch of PMC9774927 reproduces the prior quote verbatim and the finding is stable. The source entails the claim and goes beyond the single quote: (1) "TMP and SMX are small lipophilic molecules, and thus, penetration into the CSF is higher than that of beta-lactam antimicrobials or aminoglycosides"; (2) quantified CSF penetration "18% for TMP and 12% for SMX"; (3) clinical evidence of therapeutic adequacy — in 15 preoperative patients, "the CSF concentrations in 11 of 14 patients achieved levels exceeding MIC for Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis"; (4) listed indications include Listeria monocytogenes meningitis (alternative to ampicillin) and Gram-negative meningitis. One caveat for downstream use: the source frames TMP-SMX as a qualified/alternative agent for susceptible pathogens, not a universal first-line meningitis drug, and separately notes TMP-SMX is the most common antibiotic cause of drug-induced aseptic meningitis (an adverse effect, not a penetration contradiction). Net: the claim of adequate CNS/CSF penetration to treat susceptible meningitis is entailed.
